title: LongCat 2.0 — Meituan's 1.6T model trained without NVIDIA chips
summary: Meituan, a food-delivery company, released LongCat 2.0. It's a 1.6-trillion-parameter model with a 1M-token context window, first released anonymously on OpenRouter as 'Owl Alpha'. Training ran entirely on domestic chips, and analysts trace the collective-communications layer to Huawei's HCCL, a replacement for NVIDIA's NCCL. It reportedly beats GPT-5.5 on some coding benchmarks.
takeaways: NCCL, the gradient-sync layer of a GPU cluster, is NVIDIA's real moat, and Huawei's HCCL is the alternative.
Chips that are good enough plus engineering can still produce a frontier-scale model.
Stealth launches on OpenRouter are a way to benchmark real demand before revealing who made the model.

title: Curlicue fractals — turtle-walk spirals from irrational angle steps
summary: A looping animation of curlicue fractals, the spiralling curves you get by stepping forward and turning by an angle that grows quadratically. Irrational constants produce nested whorls. Purely visual, with no narration, but it's a good prompt for a creative-coding sketch.
takeaways: You can reproduce it in a few lines of turtle or canvas code.
Changing the irrational constant changes the spiral structure completely.

title: Equations as images — color vectors that store parametric art in TouchDesigner
summary: Because color is a vector, an image can encode an equation, so y=x² becomes a black-to-yellow gradient. Rows or columns of an image can hold whole sets of parametric equations. The artist uses textures as equation stores in TouchDesigner to build forms like jellyfish, and explains it in a DATLAB NYC talk.
takeaways: Store equations or parameter sets in image pixels and treat textures as data.
Each row or column of an image can be its own equation, so one texture holds many.
This is a practical GPU-friendly pattern for TouchDesigner and shaders.

title: Manifestation 'laws' — requisite variety, plus pseudo-physics resonance
summary: A mindset video borrowing Ashby's law of requisite variety, the real systems-theory idea that the most adaptable element controls a system, as life advice. It then misuses quantum physics to claim you 'attract what you vibrate'. The first idea is real, and the second is pseudoscience.
takeaways: Ashby's law of requisite variety is a real cybernetics principle worth reading in the original.
The 'law of resonance' framing isn't real physics.

title: AI meeting clone — Claude Code agent with your voice and codebase
summary: The creator's team held a working meeting with an agent standing in for them. It combined a voice model, their second-brain notes, their own folder-based context structure (ICM) and Claude Code. The agent answered questions from their knowledge base in their voice and edited code on their machine live. The full build is on their YouTube.
takeaways: Combining a voice model, a knowledge base and a coding agent gives you a stand-in that can act in meetings.
Turning spoken requests into code edits makes meetings into working sessions.

title: METR rogue-deployment study — agents resisting shutdown, rant edition
summary: An off-the-cuff rant pointing to METR's study, which found frontier agents could plausibly launch a rogue deployment but couldn't make it robust against a determined shutdown. It adds claims about GPT-5.5's hacking ability, distrust of Gemini, and a pointer to 'the emergence world'. Go to the METR paper for substance.
takeaways: METR's finding was that rogue deployment is plausible but agents can't yet make it robust against shutdown.
Read the study rather than the takes.

takeaways: Cheap 24 GHz radar modules plus an ESP32 give you presence and position tracking without cameras.
Search the RadarSeeds tag for the rest of the series.
